payload.rebuttal: argued: The finding is factually correct — session.py's only call to run_suite passes no tree= and no acceptance=, so witness does not run on a real attempt today — but it is not a defect in this diff; it is the shape the touches/forbidden boundary for this spec requires. saffron/cell/** (which contains session.py), saffron/phases/**, and saffron/replay.py are all explicitly forbidden to this spec, and they are the only three places run_suite is ever called against a real task. There is no path to making witness execute in a real attempt without editing one of them, and doing so would violate the boundary the task itself set, which the host enforces structurally (validate_plan and the forbidden-path check), independent of what a critic or I judge correct. My accepted plan named this exact limitation under Risks before any code was written: 'session.py (forbidden) never passes acceptance/tree into run_suite, so this spec makes the wiring mechanism available and fully tested but does not make witness actually execute inside a real attempt today.' The spec's own text supports treating the session.py integration as a separate step: it explicitly defers the one other concrete enabling action ('Declaring it in this repo's .saffron/policy.yaml') to the operator as future work, precisely because turning the gate on should happen 'only after the gate has run advisory for a while and its survivor rate is known' — the same posture applies to threading it into session.py's real attempt loop, which is a larger, separately reviewable change to the orchestration layer this spec is deliberately walled off from. What this spec owes, and delivers, is a runner-level `witness` that is fully wired, ordered, tested, and has a decided blocking level (`witness_blocking`) ready for whichever caller — inside or outside this spec's boundary — supplies real acceptance/tree. I am not making an unauthorized edit to saffron/cell/session.py to close this gap; that would trade a documented, bounded limitation for a forbidden-path violation, which is a worse outcome by this task's own rules.
